headline: Hypotheses are testable predictions—educated guesses that can be proven right or wrong
universal_truth: Ideas that can't be tested can't be improved; make your beliefs falsifiable
fun_facts: A good hypothesis must be falsifiable—there must be a possible result that would prove it wrong
Einstein's relativity made specific predictions that could have disproven it—they didn't
Many business ideas fail because they were never tested as hypotheses before full commitment
discussion_questions: What assumptions are you making that you haven't tested?
How would you know if your current beliefs were wrong?
What experiments could test your important assumptions?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: A hypothesis is an educated guess you can test. 'This will work' is a hope. 'If I do X, Y will happen' is a hypothesis. The difference? Hypotheses can be proven wrong—and that's what makes them useful.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: We often hold beliefs without testing them. Why is testability so valuable?

options.text: Testable ideas can be improved or discarded—if you can't test a belief, you can't know if it's wrong; untestable ideas can persist forever without improving or correcting
options.response: Yes. Testability enables learning. If there's no way to be wrong, there's no way to get righter. Making ideas testable is making them improvable.
Confirmation is part of it, but more importantly, testing allows falsification—proving ideas wrong...

q1.title: Falsifiability
q1.script: A good hypothesis can be proven wrong. That might seem like weakness, but it's strength. Ideas that can't be wrong can never be tested, corrected, or trusted.

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Prediction Making
q2.script: Good hypotheses make predictions: 'If X, then Y.' This creates tests. If Y happens, the hypothesis is supported. If not-Y happens, the hypothesis is challenged.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Life Hypotheses
q3.script: You have hypotheses about life: 'If I work hard, I'll succeed.' 'If I'm kind, people will like me.' Are these tested? What evidence would prove them wrong?
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Ideas that can't be tested can't be improved. Make your beliefs falsifiable. Test your hypotheses.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 295. Tomorrow, we'll explore asking nature questions—scientific inquiry. Until then, turn one of your assumptions into a testable hypothesis.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Hypothesis Formation - What Can You Test?
growTrack.activity: Pick an assumption you're making about work, relationships, or life. Formulate it as a hypothesis: 'If I do X, Y will happen.' What evidence would support or refute it? How could you test it?
